source.title: Understanding the double descent curve in Machine Learning
source.authors: Luis Sacouto; J. M. Ramos; Miguel Almeida; A. Wichert

record.file_problem: None; the supplied text contains the full paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments that challenge a simple account of double descent: in its neural-network experiments, the apparent second descent follows the change in initialization and weight reuse, and disappears or shifts when those choices change.
record.gate_note: Reports neural-network experiments on MNIST with weight reuse, early stopping and small-weight initialization, plus feature-based Random ReLU experiments. The MNIST network curves are described in text but their numerical values are figure-only. The feature-based results concern linear regression on fixed features, not the natural-label generalization versions listed. No results are reported for random-label fitting, network width sweeps beyond interpolation with comparable training recipes, architecture comparisons, optimizer comparisons, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples.
record.test_reason: The experiments concern double descent and sensitivity to norm constraints, initialization, weight reuse and stopping. They do not establish V2's defining comparison: widening learned ReLU networks beyond an empirically identified zero-training-error width under training to convergence. The paper's parameter-count threshold N×K cannot substitute for that comparison. No other listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors attribute fixed-feature double descent to a bias toward low-norm solutions, argue that initialization and stopping explain the tested neural-network regime changes, and recommend overparameterized models when learning favors less-overfitted solutions. These are their interpretations, not demonstrations that every listed generalization claim holds or fails.
record.recipe_differences: The paper investigates double descent through Random ReLU feature regression and MNIST neural-network experiments that vary weight reuse, initialization and early stopping; it does not reproduce the claim versions' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: In the neural-network experiments, the apparent regime change follows the point where weight reuse is switched off. In the feature-based experiments, performance changes with the norm-target distance R and regularization strength λ.

fits_no_version.finding: In fixed Random ReLU feature regression, biasing solutions toward higher-norm targets worsens post-threshold test loss; stronger L2 regularization removes the overfitting peak while increasing training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent in the tested fixed-feature regression depends on solution selection and regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Continuing neural-network weight reuse worsens performance beyond the theoretical threshold, and moving the reuse switch moves the second descent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The apparent neural-network double-descent transition can depend on initialization and training history rather than the N×K parameter threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger networks initialized with small weights and trained with early stopping tend to perform better on the tested MNIST subset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing network width can improve generalization under small initialization and early stopping.

record.code_released: Code and data available by email request to the first author.
record.problems: The neural-network evidence is limited to a MNIST subset and qualitative figure descriptions; exact plotted values and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The text gives no explicit controls or capability checks. The feature-based experiments use fixed features and linear regression, so they do not establish the claim versions about neural networks trained on natural labels.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance compared with natural-label training.

Test error beyond the width attaining zero training error in learned one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained to convergence without explicit regularization. Activation, convergence and the empirical fitting threshold are not established.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under the specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Qualitative results explicitly stated in the text are usable without exact figure values. The decisive limitation for V2 is the missing post-zero-training-error, convergence-conditioned comparison, rather than the absence of numerical curve coordinates.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label versus random-label test comparison.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep testing test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison of gap predictors.
No memorized-example removal and retraining comparison.

rows.subject: Random ReLU features with linear output layer
rows.size_stated: 3000 images; 784 pixels; 10 possible classes; feature count varied
rows.operation_detail: Varied number of features and selected solutions using a penalty toward a point p of norm R; collected train and test squared errors.
rows.measure: Training and test squared errors versus number of parameters
rows.value: For higher R, post-threshold test performance deteriorates and approaches the bias-variance prediction.
rows.locator: Experiments, Results on feature-based models, Figure 7 and accompanying text
rows.note: This tests the paper's explanation of double descent in a feature-based linear model; it does not test any listed claim version.
rows.check: The qualitative result is accurately recorded, but concerns fixed random features with a fitted linear output and an explicit penalty. It does not measure any listed version; observed is not a version-relative state here.

rows.subject: Random ReLU features with linear output layer
rows.size_stated: 3000 images; 784 pixels; 10 possible classes; feature count varied
rows.operation_detail: Increased l2 regularization strength λ while collecting training and test losses across feature counts.
rows.measure: Training and test losses versus number of features
rows.value: As λ increases, the overfitting peak disappears and double descent becomes a single descent; training error increases while generalization improves.
rows.locator: Experiments, Results on feature-based models, Figure 8 and accompanying text
rows.note: Figure 8 values are not given numerically; the qualitative outcome is stated in text.
rows.check: The regularization result is accurately paraphrased but measures fixed-feature regression, not a listed version.

rows.subject: Neural network; hidden-layer size increased with weight reuse
rows.size_stated: MNIST subset of 4200 images; hidden-layer size varied; other size not stated
rows.stage_stated: trained over a large number of epochs; reused trained weights; stopping details vary by experiment
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the network-size experiment while continuing weight reuse past the proposed threshold.
rows.measure: Train and test losses as network size increases
rows.value: Without the early-stopping constraint, performance degrades further; passing the threshold seems to have no impact.
rows.locator: Results on neural networks, The second descent is a product of the early stopping constraint, Figure 9 and accompanying text
rows.note: The text describes performance qualitatively; exact plotted values are unavailable.
rows.check: The text explicitly reports deteriorating performance, so the qualitative result is readable. Its link to V2 remains indeterminate because the experiment uses cumulative weight reuse and a theoretical parameter-count threshold without identifying the width attaining zero training error or documenting convergence.

rows.subject: Neural network; weight-reuse switch varied
rows.size_stated: MNIST subset of 4200 images; three performance curves; other size not stated
rows.stage_stated: trained with weight reuse until a varied switch point
rows.operation_detail: Varied the model complexity at which the weight-reuse scheme was switched off.
rows.value: The second descent occurs at the switch point, not at the theoretical over-parameterization threshold.
rows.locator: Results on neural networks, The threshold does not predict the regime change, Figure 10 and accompanying text
rows.note: Exact values are figure-only; the location of the regime change is described in text.
rows.check: The stated switch-point result is readable, but locating a second descent relative to an initialization change does not test V2's post-fit widening claim. V2 does not assert a test-error peak at N×K parameters.

rows.subject: Neural networks trained with early stopping
rows.size_stated: MNIST subset of 4200 images; network complexity varied
rows.stage_stated: initialized with small random weights and trained with early stopping
rows.operation_detail: Repeated training with early stopping while increasing network size.
rows.measure: Train and test losses as network complexity increases
rows.value: Performance tends to improve as complexity increases; the authors say the curve confirms that over-parameterized networks with weight constraint perform best.
rows.locator: Results on neural networks, Over-parameterized with constraint is best, Figure 11 and accompanying text
rows.note: Qualitative trend only; no numerical values are stated.
rows.check: The text clearly states improving performance with increasing complexity; missing numerical values alone do not make that trend unreadable. However, early-stopped training without an identified zero-training-error width does not establish V2's convergence-conditioned effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
